curriculum: NaCCA Religious and Moral Education Curriculum for Primary Schools (September 2019)
code_note: The curriculum prints these as B2. 4.1.1.1, B2. 4.1.1.2 and B2. 4.1.1.3; normalized here with no spaces for consistency.
accessibility_note: Teachers may read prompts aloud. Accept oral, written, drawn or role-play responses where suitable. Assess curriculum knowledge and reasoning, not a learner's personal religious belief or practice. Scenarios do not require attendance at a worship site.

indicators.statement: Identify things that families do to show their commitment to God.

questions.prompt: Which is an example of a family activity that may show commitment to God?
questions.hint: Think of an activity families may do to worship or pray.
questions.explanation: The curriculum names prayer and worship among ways families may show commitment to God.
questions.misconception_note: Do not assume every family follows the same practice.

questions.prompt: A family goes together to church, a mosque or a shrine. What kind of activity is this?
questions.hint: Where do people gather for worship?
questions.explanation: The curriculum gives going to a church, mosque or shrine as examples of family religious activities.
questions.misconception_note: All three are valid examples in the curriculum; avoid ranking religions.

questions.prompt: Write or say two things a family may do to show commitment to God.
questions.hint: Use two activities from lessons or the examples in class.
questions.explanation: Families may show commitment through religious activities such as prayer, worship and giving.
questions.misconception_note: Accept relevant examples without requiring the learner's own family to practise them.

criteria.description: Any two suitable examples: prayer, worship, attending church/mosque/shrine, fasting, offering/offertory, Sadaqah or Zakat.

questions.prompt: Which example of giving is named in the curriculum as a way of showing commitment to God?
questions.hint: It is a form of giving mentioned alongside Zakat.
questions.explanation: The curriculum lists Sadaqah and Zakat among examples of family religious practices.
questions.misconception_note: The question identifies an example; it does not ask learners to judge another person's practice.

questions.prompt: Which practice is listed in the curriculum as an example of family commitment to God?
questions.hint: It is a form of giving named in the lesson examples.
questions.explanation: Zakat is one of the examples listed in the curriculum.
questions.misconception_note: Keep the focus on recognising the curriculum example, not comparing faiths.

questions.prompt: Tell one example of a religious activity that a family might do in the morning.
questions.hint: Think of the example about the start of the day.
questions.explanation: Morning devotion is an example of a family religious activity in the curriculum.
questions.misconception_note: Accept other reasonable answers and do not require disclosure about home life.

criteria.description: A suitable response such as morning devotion or prayer.

questions.prompt: Match each activity to the best description: (1) family prayer, (2) family football game. Descriptions: A. religious activity; B. recreation.
questions.hint: Which activity is worship or devotion?
questions.explanation: Prayer is a religious activity; a football game is recreation.
questions.misconception_note: A family may do both kinds of activity; the categories describe the activity, not the family.

criteria.description: Matches 1 with A.
Matches 2 with B.

questions.prompt: A family fasts as part of its religious practice. Is this an example of commitment to God? Answer yes or no and give a reason.
questions.hint: Look at the activities listed in the indicator examples.
questions.explanation: The curriculum includes fasting as an example.
questions.misconception_note: No learner should be asked to fast for this assessment.

criteria.description: Yes; fasting is named among the examples of religious practices that show commitment.

questions.prompt: Which action best fits the idea of worship in the lesson?
options: A child tears a classmate's work
A family hides litter in a room
A learner refuses to share class materials
questions.hint: Choose the action connected to expressing devotion to God.
questions.explanation: Worship is explicitly named as one way a family may show commitment to God.
questions.misconception_note: Do not imply that worship is the only way families show commitment.

questions.prompt: Draw one respectful, non-specific example of a family religious activity. Add a label or explain your picture orally.
questions.hint: You may draw people praying or gathering for devotion without showing a particular religion.
questions.explanation: The task checks whether the learner can identify a family religious activity.
questions.misconception_note: Do not assess artistic skill or require religious symbols.

criteria.description: A drawing that clearly represents an appropriate activity, such as family prayer or worship; accept a spoken explanation.

questions.prompt: The class is sorting family religious activities into daily, weekly and occasional activities. Which is a useful first step?
options: Ask how often each activity happens
questions.answer: Ask how often each activity happens
questions.hint: The groups should be based on frequency.
questions.explanation: The curriculum asks learners to identify how often activities occur during a day, week or occasionally.
questions.misconception_note: Families can have different routines; do not assume one schedule fits all.

questions.prompt: Ama's group is making a chart. They place their example of morning devotion under 'daily' because their family does it each morning. What should they do next?
questions.hint: The chart describes how often the activity happens for the family being discussed.
questions.explanation: Learners classify activities by their frequency, without assuming all families follow the same routine.
questions.misconception_note: Avoid treating one learner's household routine as universal.

criteria.description: Record that frequency for their example and allow other families' examples to be different.

questions.prompt: Name one place, mentioned in the curriculum, where a family may go together for worship.
questions.hint: There are three examples in the indicator activities.
questions.explanation: The curriculum names a church, mosque and shrine as possible worship places.
questions.misconception_note: Accept any one; do not require a visit.

questions.prompt: In pairs, act out a brief scene showing a family preparing for a religious activity. You may use a made-up family and a general activity such as prayer or worship.
questions.hint: Show the activity clearly and treat every person's practice respectfully.
questions.explanation: Role-play is an exemplar activity for identifying family practices that show commitment to God.
questions.misconception_note: Do not make learners perform actual worship or imitate a faith disrespectfully.

criteria.description: activity is identifiable
scene treats people and practices respectfully
learner explains the example

questions.prompt: Which pair contains two examples listed for family commitment to God?
questions.hint: Look for two religious practices from the lesson list.
questions.explanation: Prayer and fasting are both named as examples.
questions.misconception_note: This is a recognition task, not a test of personal religious practice.

questions.prompt: Choose one family religious activity and explain in one sentence how it shows commitment to God.
questions.hint: Say what the family is doing and what it expresses.
questions.explanation: Commitment can be shown through taking part in religious activities.
questions.misconception_note: Accept a general example; do not ask the learner to reveal private beliefs.

criteria.description: Any reasonable explanation linking the activity to worship, devotion, prayer or religious observance.

questions.prompt: A family gives an offering during its religious practice. Which curriculum example is this closest to?
questions.hint: The word is listed with worship and prayer.
questions.explanation: The curriculum includes offertory among the examples of religious activities.
questions.misconception_note: Spelling variants such as offering may be accepted where appropriate.

questions.prompt: Sort these sample activities into 'daily', 'weekly' or 'occasionally' based only on the schedule the teacher gives: morning devotion (each morning), family worship gathering (each week), special religious celebration (once a year).
questions.hint: Use the schedule in brackets, not a guess about every family.
questions.explanation: The indicator asks learners to consider how often family religious activities occur.
questions.misconception_note: The schedules are practice examples and are not claims about all families.

criteria.description: one point for each correctly sorted activity
uses the given schedule

questions.prompt: Complete the sentence: A family may show commitment to God through prayer, worship and ___. Give one suitable example.
questions.hint: Choose another practice from the curriculum examples.
questions.explanation: The curriculum includes several forms of religious practice and giving.
questions.misconception_note: Accept other relevant examples taught in class.

criteria.description: A suitable example such as fasting, giving/offertory, Sadaqah or Zakat.

questions.prompt: Two learners describe different religious activities their families do. What is a respectful way to respond?
questions.hint: Think about respect for different family practices.
questions.explanation: The indicator identifies practices; respectful discussion allows for different family routines and traditions.
questions.misconception_note: Do not suggest one family's practice is the only acceptable one.

criteria.description: Listen politely, recognise that families may practise differently, and avoid mocking or ranking their activities.

indicators.content_standard: Describe the roles of the family and community in their daily lives

skills.description: Recognise the examples and vocabulary in the lesson.
Explain meanings and connections in an example.
Apply the lesson to a situation and justify a choice.
Communicate understanding through a performance, drawing or demonstration.

spec.difficultyPlan: 5 foundational, 7 simple-use, 5 application and 3 challenge questions.

indicators.statement: Explain the need for commitment to God.

questions.prompt: According to the curriculum examples, why do people need to be committed to God?
options: It is a command from God
It gives permission to hurt others
questions.answer: It is a command from God
questions.hint: One reason in the lesson is about what God asks people to do.
questions.explanation: The curriculum lists that commitment to God is a command from God.
questions.misconception_note: Present this as the curriculum's religious teaching, not a demand that learners state their personal belief.

questions.prompt: Which benefit of commitment to God is named in the curriculum?
options: It guarantees a learner will never face difficulty
It removes the need to respect others
It means a person never makes mistakes
questions.hint: Choose the benefit stated in the indicator examples.
questions.explanation: The curriculum gives attracting blessings from God as a reason for commitment.
questions.misconception_note: Do not turn the curriculum statement into a promise of guaranteed outcomes.

questions.prompt: In your own words, what does commitment mean?
questions.hint: Think of being devoted and dependable.
questions.explanation: Learners are guided to explain the meaning of commitment before discussing why people are committed to God.
questions.misconception_note: Accept age-appropriate wording; do not require theological definitions.

criteria.description: A suitable explanation: being dedicated, faithful or devoted to something and continuing to take it seriously.

questions.prompt: Give one reason from the lesson why a person may be committed to God.
questions.hint: There are two reasons listed in the curriculum.
questions.explanation: Both reasons are given in the curriculum examples.
questions.misconception_note: Accept either reason; the learner need not personally affirm it.

criteria.description: It is a command from God, or it attracts blessings from God.

questions.prompt: A learner says, 'People may be committed to God because the curriculum says it is a command from God.' Which idea is the learner giving?
options: A reason to break a promise
questions.hint: The sentence explains why someone may do something.
questions.explanation: The statement repeats one of the reasons listed in the curriculum.
questions.misconception_note: Distinguish reporting a teaching from judging classmates' beliefs.

questions.prompt: Explain orally one benefit of commitment to God that is named in the lesson.
questions.hint: Use a reason or benefit from the lesson.
questions.explanation: The curriculum names blessings from God as a reason and invites learners to discuss personal examples.
questions.misconception_note: Accept an explanation without asking the learner to disclose personal faith.

criteria.description: The learner states that it attracts blessings from God, or gives another relevant benefit from class discussion.

questions.prompt: Match each statement with its category: (1) 'It is a command from God'; (2) 'It attracts blessings from God'. Categories: A. reason for commitment; B. benefit/reason named for commitment.
questions.hint: Both ideas support the need for commitment; notice whether the statement is a command or a benefit.
questions.explanation: The curriculum presents both as reasons to be committed to God.
questions.misconception_note: The labels are for organising the lesson content; both are valid curriculum points.

criteria.description: Matches 1 with A.
Matches 2 with B.

questions.prompt: Kofi is asked why people discuss commitment to God in class. Which response best uses the lesson?
options: The lesson says it is a command from God and it attracts blessings from God.
It teaches people to disrespect one another.
It means no one should ask questions.
It is only about winning games.
questions.answer: The lesson says it is a command from God and it attracts blessings from God.
questions.hint: Recall the two reasons listed in the curriculum.
questions.explanation: This answer includes both curriculum reasons.
questions.misconception_note: Keep answers grounded in the lesson's stated points.

questions.prompt: Does commitment mean doing something only once and then forgetting it? Explain briefly.
questions.hint: Use the meaning of commitment discussed in class.
questions.explanation: Commitment involves dedication and taking something seriously over time.
questions.misconception_note: Do not demand a specific religious routine as proof of commitment.

criteria.description: No. Commitment means being dedicated or devoted, rather than treating it as a one-time action and forgetting it.

questions.prompt: Which answer best explains why commitment to God is discussed in the curriculum?
options: The curriculum says it is a command from God and may attract blessings from God
It helps people avoid all responsibilities
It proves that other people are wrong
It is a way to tease classmates
questions.answer: The curriculum says it is a command from God and may attract blessings from God
questions.hint: Choose the answer that uses the lesson's reasons respectfully.
questions.explanation: The indicator examples give these two reasons.
questions.misconception_note: Reject claims that commitment is a reason to demean others.

questions.prompt: Say one reason for commitment to God using the phrase 'According to the lesson…'.
questions.hint: Begin with the words given in the prompt.
questions.explanation: This phrasing lets learners report the curriculum respectfully without being assessed on personal belief.
questions.misconception_note: Do not score personal agreement or disagreement.

criteria.description: Example: 'According to the lesson, commitment to God is a command from God' or '…attracts blessings from God.'

questions.prompt: The teacher asks learners to share an example of commitment at home, school or in the community. Which response fits the activity?
options: Give a suitable example of a religious activity, if comfortable
Insist every learner has the same experience
questions.answer: Give a suitable example of a religious activity, if comfortable
questions.hint: The activity invites sharing personal experiences, but sharing should be respectful and safe.
questions.explanation: The curriculum invites learners to share experiences from home, school, a worship place or community.
questions.misconception_note: Learners may use a general or fictional example instead of disclosing private information.

questions.prompt: A classmate does not want to describe a private family religious practice. What should you do?
questions.hint: Personal sharing should not be forced.
questions.explanation: The curriculum encourages sharing experiences, but assessment should focus on understanding rather than private disclosure.
questions.misconception_note: Do not treat silence about private practice as lack of knowledge.

criteria.description: Respect the classmate's choice and allow a general or fictional example instead.

questions.prompt: Name one activity a person may do to show commitment to God, and give one reason from the lesson for commitment.
questions.hint: Give one activity and one reason; they are different parts of the answer.
questions.explanation: The indicator covers personal examples of commitment and reasons for it.
questions.misconception_note: Accept suitable examples without assuming the learner performs them personally.

criteria.description: Any suitable religious activity (such as prayer, worship or fasting) plus either 'it is a command from God' or 'it attracts blessings from God.'

questions.prompt: Which statement goes beyond the reasons given in the curriculum and should not be treated as a lesson fact?
options: Commitment guarantees that a person will never have a problem
Commitment is described as a command from God
Commitment may attract blessings from God
Learners can discuss examples of commitment
questions.answer: Commitment guarantees that a person will never have a problem
questions.hint: Look for an absolute promise that is not stated in the lesson.
questions.explanation: The curriculum mentions blessings but does not promise freedom from every difficulty.
questions.misconception_note: Avoid turning religious benefits into guaranteed material or health outcomes.

questions.prompt: Draw a simple picture or symbol that can represent dedication or commitment. Explain how it represents the idea; it need not show a religious symbol.
questions.hint: You might draw someone keeping a promise or caring for something regularly.
questions.explanation: The curriculum asks learners to explain the meaning of commitment; a general symbol can demonstrate understanding.
questions.misconception_note: Do not require a religious image or assess drawing ability.

criteria.description: A suitable symbol or scene with a reasonable explanation linking it to dedication, faithfulness or devotion.

questions.prompt: Complete this idea: People in the lesson are encouraged to be committed to God because ___.
questions.hint: Use one of the two reasons given in the curriculum.
questions.explanation: Both reasons appear in the indicator exemplars.
questions.misconception_note: Accept either reason.

criteria.description: It is a command from God; or it attracts blessings from God.

questions.prompt: In pairs, role-play a respectful question-and-answer in which one learner asks why people may be committed to God and the other gives one reason from the lesson.
questions.hint: Use either 'a command from God' or 'it attracts blessings from God.'
questions.explanation: The curriculum suggests discussion and questions and answers about commitment.
questions.misconception_note: Learners report the lesson content; no one has to claim a particular belief.

criteria.description: gives a relevant reason
listens and responds respectfully
communicates clearly

questions.prompt: Which is the best short summary of the lesson's reasons for commitment to God?
options: It is a command from God and it attracts blessings from God
It is only a way to compete with others
It means families never need to help one another
It is unrelated to religious life
questions.answer: It is a command from God and it attracts blessings from God
questions.hint: Choose the answer containing the two listed reasons.
questions.explanation: The two reasons are stated in the curriculum examples.
questions.misconception_note: Avoid adding claims not stated by the curriculum.

questions.prompt: Give a short oral or written explanation of commitment to God. Include what commitment means and one reason for it from the lesson.
questions.hint: Answer in two parts: meaning, then reason.
questions.explanation: This combines the two teaching steps in the indicator exemplars.
questions.misconception_note: Assess understanding, not the learner's own belief or religious identity.

criteria.description: explains dedication/devotion
gives one curriculum reason
understandable response

indicators.content_standard: Describe the roles of the family and community in their daily lives

skills.description: Recognise the examples and vocabulary in the lesson.
Explain meanings and connections in an example.
Apply the lesson to a situation and justify a choice.
Communicate understanding through a performance, drawing or demonstration.

spec.difficultyPlan: 5 foundational, 7 simple-use, 5 application and 3 challenge questions.

indicators.statement: Describe factors that promote good relationships between children and their parents.

questions.prompt: Which behaviour helps promote a good relationship between a child and a parent?
questions.hint: Choose a positive behaviour named in the lesson.
questions.explanation: Respect is one of the factors listed in the curriculum.
questions.misconception_note: Respect does not mean a child must remain silent about unsafe situations.

questions.prompt: Which factor from the lesson can help a child and parent have a good relationship?
questions.hint: It is a caring feeling named in the list.
questions.explanation: Love is listed as a factor promoting good parent-child relationships.
questions.misconception_note: Accept love shown through caring, kind actions, not only words.

questions.prompt: Name two factors that promote good relationships between children and their parents.
questions.hint: There are six examples in the curriculum list.
questions.explanation: These behaviours and attitudes are listed as factors promoting good relationships.
questions.misconception_note: Accept other relevant factors taught in class.

criteria.description: Any two: comportment, respect, love, obedience, humility or friendliness.

questions.prompt: Kojo disagrees with a parent about a household task. Which response is most likely to support a good relationship?
questions.hint: Choose an action that shows respect and good comportment.
questions.explanation: Respect and comportment are factors in good relationships.
questions.misconception_note: A respectful conversation can include disagreement; obedience is not the only factor.

questions.prompt: Which word from the curriculum list means following a reasonable instruction?
questions.hint: It is one of the attitudes named in the indicator.
questions.explanation: Obedience is listed as a factor that promotes good parent-child relationships.
questions.misconception_note: Do not frame obedience as requiring a child to follow unsafe instructions.

questions.prompt: Choose one factor from the lesson and explain how it may help a child and parent get along well.
questions.hint: Say the factor, then describe a helpful action that shows it.
questions.explanation: The indicator asks learners to describe factors, not just list them.
questions.misconception_note: Accept safe, practical examples; a learner need not share personal family details.

criteria.description: A reasonable explanation connecting respect, love, obedience, humility, friendliness or comportment with a positive relationship.

questions.prompt: Match each action to the factor it shows: (1) greeting a parent kindly; (2) speaking politely and listening; (3) doing a reasonable agreed task. Factors: A. friendliness; B. respect; C. obedience/responsibility.
questions.hint: Look at the main quality shown by each action.
questions.explanation: Friendly greetings, respectful speech and following reasonable agreed instructions can support good relationships.
questions.misconception_note: Some actions may show more than one positive quality; accept a justified alternative.

criteria.description: Matches 1 with A.
Matches 2 with B.
Matches 3 with C.

questions.prompt: Which action best shows humility in a family relationship?
options: Admitting a mistake and being willing to learn
Bragging that nobody can correct you
Blaming someone else for every mistake
questions.answer: Admitting a mistake and being willing to learn
questions.hint: Humility includes not acting as if you can never be wrong.
questions.explanation: Humility is named among the factors promoting good relationships.
questions.misconception_note: Humility does not mean thinking you have no worth.

questions.prompt: Give one example of a friendly action a child could show toward a parent.
questions.hint: Think of a kind way to greet or speak to someone.
questions.explanation: Friendliness is one factor listed in the curriculum.
questions.misconception_note: Accept age-appropriate examples.

criteria.description: Any suitable example such as greeting warmly, speaking kindly, offering help or sharing a pleasant conversation.

questions.prompt: A parent reminds Esi to put away her books. Which response best supports a good relationship?
options: She puts them away or calmly explains if she needs help
She hides the books and lies
questions.answer: She puts them away or calmly explains if she needs help
questions.hint: Look for comportment, respect and a helpful response.
questions.explanation: Respectful communication and appropriate conduct can promote good relationships.
questions.misconception_note: The prompt is about a routine, reasonable request, not unsafe demands.

questions.prompt: Which behaviour is least likely to promote a good parent-child relationship?
questions.hint: Choose the behaviour opposite to trust and good conduct.
questions.explanation: The listed positive factors include respect, love, humility, friendliness, obedience and comportment; dishonesty undermines a good relationship.
questions.misconception_note: Focus on behaviour, not on labelling a child as a bad person.

questions.prompt: Draw a simple scene showing one factor that helps children and parents have a good relationship. Label the factor or explain the drawing orally.
questions.hint: You could show a kind greeting or a respectful conversation.
questions.explanation: The activity checks recognition of factors that promote good parent-child relationships.
questions.misconception_note: Assess the idea, not drawing quality or a learner's actual family situation.

criteria.description: A clear scene showing one factor such as respect, love, friendliness, humility, obedience or good comportment.

questions.prompt: In pairs, act out a short, respectful scene between a child and parent showing friendliness or respect during an everyday conversation.
questions.hint: Use a simple situation such as greeting, asking for help or discussing a task.
questions.explanation: The curriculum recommends dramatizing behaviours that show good relationships.
questions.misconception_note: Do not use frightening, humiliating or unsafe scenarios.

criteria.description: clearly demonstrates a relevant factor
dialogue/actions are respectful
learner names or explains the factor

questions.prompt: What is one way good comportment can help a child and parent get along?
questions.hint: Think about how a person's behaviour affects others.
questions.explanation: Comportment is named in the curriculum list of relationship-promoting factors.
questions.misconception_note: Accept age-appropriate explanations rather than requiring a dictionary definition.

criteria.description: A suitable explanation: behaving appropriately, speaking calmly or acting considerately helps reduce conflict and supports cooperation.

questions.prompt: A child listens while a parent explains a household rule, then asks a question politely. Which factor is most clearly shown?
questions.hint: The child listens and speaks politely.
questions.explanation: Respectful listening and speech can promote a good relationship.
questions.misconception_note: Listening does not prevent a child from asking questions or sharing concerns.

questions.prompt: Yaw accidentally spills water. He admits what happened and offers to help clean it safely. Which two factors can his actions show?
questions.hint: He tells the truth about the mistake and responds helpfully.
questions.explanation: Admitting a mistake can show humility; responding appropriately shows good comportment.
questions.misconception_note: The cleanup should be safe and supervised if needed.

questions.prompt: Name one behaviour you would like to see in a good parent-child relationship and say why it helps.
questions.hint: Choose from the lesson list and add a reason.
questions.explanation: Learners identify and discuss behaviours that promote good relationships.
questions.misconception_note: Allow a general answer rather than asking learners to evaluate their own family.

criteria.description: Any relevant factor and a reasonable explanation, such as respect helps people listen to each other.

questions.prompt: Which group contains only factors listed in the curriculum for promoting good parent-child relationships?
questions.hint: Check each word against the lesson list.
questions.explanation: Respect, love and friendliness are all named in the curriculum.
questions.misconception_note: The listed factors are examples, not the only ways to build healthy relationships.

questions.prompt: Write, say or draw two behaviours that promote good relationships between children and parents. Explain one of them.
questions.hint: You need two factors and one explanation.
questions.explanation: This checks both identification and description of relationship-promoting factors.
questions.misconception_note: Do not require personal family examples.

criteria.description: one point per relevant factor
explains one factor with a sensible example
response is understandable

questions.prompt: A child feels upset about a parent's decision. Which action can help keep the relationship respectful while sharing the child's feelings?
options: Explain the feelings calmly and listen to the response
questions.answer: Explain the feelings calmly and listen to the response
questions.hint: Good relationships can include disagreement handled with respect.
questions.explanation: Respect, good comportment and communication support relationships even when people disagree.
questions.misconception_note: If a child feels unsafe, they should seek help from a trusted adult; respectful discussion is for ordinary disagreements.

indicators.content_standard: Describe the roles of the family and community in their daily lives

skills.description: Recognise the examples and vocabulary in the lesson.
Explain meanings and connections in an example.
Communicate understanding through a performance, drawing or demonstration.

spec.difficultyPlan: 5 foundational, 7 simple-use, 5 application and 3 challenge questions.

indicators.statement: Describe ways of promoting personal hygiene and safety in the community.
indicators.content_standard: Identify ways of caring for the body

questions.prompt: You have finished playing and are about to eat. Which pair will help you clean your hands?
questions.hint: Think about what can wash dirt away.
questions.explanation: Soap and clean water help wash dirt off your hands before you touch food.

questions.prompt: What does a toothbrush help a person clean?
questions.hint: Which part of the body do you use to chew?
questions.explanation: Use a toothbrush with toothpaste to clean the surfaces of the teeth.

questions.prompt: Which item makes light beside a community road after dark? Complete the words “street ___”.
questions.hint: Think about what allows people to see the path.
questions.explanation: A street light helps people see where they are walking.

questions.prompt: Which activity helps keep clothes clean?
questions.hint: Which choice takes dirt out of the cloth?
questions.explanation: Washing removes dirt. Folding changes the shape but leaves dirt in the cloth.

questions.prompt: Which adult could a pupil tell about broken glass on the school path?
questions.hint: Choose someone who can arrange safe help.
questions.explanation: A teacher can keep pupils away and arrange for an adult to remove the glass.

questions.prompt: Draw two things you would put beside a handwashing place. Label them or tell your teacher their names.
questions.hint: What will wet the hands, and what will help lift dirt?
questions.explanation: Water and soap together let a person wash dirty hands.

criteria.description: Shows clean water or a tap.
Shows soap and names both items.

questions.prompt: Tell a partner when you would wash your hands during a school day. Explain one choice.
questions.hint: Think about something you do just before lunch.
questions.explanation: After using the toilet, wash your hands. Clean hands also help keep food clean before eating.

criteria.description: Names a suitable time such as after using the toilet or before eating.
Connects washing with keeping hands or food clean.

questions.prompt: Kojo has a dirty shirt and a clean shirt. Where should he put the dirty shirt until it is washed?
questions.hint: Keep the two kinds of clothing apart.
questions.explanation: Use the laundry place so the dirty shirt can be washed separately from clean clothes.

questions.prompt: Using pretend soap and water, show your partner how to wash and dry your hands.
questions.hint: Think about how to remove the soap at the end.
questions.explanation: Wet and soap the hands, rub the surfaces, rinse, and dry them cleanly.

criteria.description: Mimes wetting, applying soap and rubbing the hands.
Mimes rinsing and drying with a clean item or air.

questions.prompt: After a game, Ama has muddy skin. Which action cleans her body?
questions.hint: Look for an action that washes her skin.
questions.explanation: Bathing helps remove sweat and dirt from the skin.

questions.prompt: Pretend you see a broken street light on the way home with an adult. Show what you could say.
questions.hint: Give a clue that helps the adult find the spot.
questions.explanation: Tell the adult where the light is broken. Let adults arrange the repair.

criteria.description: Reports the light to a trusted adult.
Identifies its location without touching the light or wires.

questions.prompt: Who should clear a deep, blocked gutter outside school?
questions.hint: Think about who can deal with a deep gutter safely.
questions.explanation: A pupil can report it from a safe place. Equipped adults can clear the blockage.

questions.prompt: Draw a safe route past a patch of broken glass. Add someone who can help.
questions.hint: Can the walker stay away and still tell someone?
questions.explanation: Walk around the hazard and tell a trusted adult where it is.

criteria.description: Marks a route that stays away from the glass.
Shows or names a trusted adult who can arrange help.

questions.prompt: A class has a toothbrush, a broom, toothpaste and a dustpan. Make one pair for body care and another for cleaning a classroom.
questions.hint: Look for two things that work together.
questions.explanation: Toothpaste goes with the toothbrush. A broom sweeps litter into a dustpan.

criteria.description: Pairs toothbrush and toothpaste for teeth.
Pairs broom and dustpan for the classroom.

questions.prompt: Kofi wore a clean shirt but has mud on his hands. What is still needed before he eats, and why?
questions.hint: Think about which part touches the food.
questions.explanation: Hands touch food. They still need washing even when the shirt is already clean.

criteria.description: Suggests washing hands with soap and clean water.
Explains that changing clothes has not cleaned his hands.

questions.prompt: Show how to leave a pretend classroom floor ready for walking after tidying light paper litter.
questions.hint: Look at what might still be in a walker's way when the job is done.
questions.explanation: Remove light litter, then put tools away so nobody trips.

criteria.description: Demonstrates safely sweeping the paper into a dustpan or bin.
Returns the cleaning items so the walkway is clear.

questions.prompt: Make a two-picture reminder for a younger pupil. Show a time to clean teeth and a time to wash hands.
questions.hint: Think about getting ready in the morning and getting ready to eat.
questions.explanation: A morning toothbrush picture and a handwashing picture before a meal show two ways to care for the body.

criteria.description: Shows brushing teeth as part of a daily routine.
Shows handwashing at an appropriate time and labels or explains both.

questions.prompt: Your class is having a clean-up. There are paper scraps on the floor and a sharp tin outside. Plan what pupils can do and what an adult should handle.
questions.hint: Are the two items equally safe to pick up?
questions.explanation: Pupils can help tidy paper. A sharp tin needs adult attention.

criteria.description: Chooses light paper for a supervised pupil task.
Leaves the sharp tin alone and reports it to an adult.

questions.prompt: A friend says a tidy road is always safe after dark. Give a reason to check the lighting as well as the ground.
questions.hint: Think of a clean path you still cannot see well.
questions.explanation: A swept path can be dark. Good lighting helps people see where they are going.

criteria.description: Acknowledges that clearing litter removes one hazard.
Explains why light helps people see the path or another hazard.

questions.prompt: Plan a class reminder with two jobs for the day, one for clean bodies and one for a safe shared space. Tell who can do each job.
questions.hint: Ask how each job helps a person or the whole group.
questions.explanation: Pupils might wash before lunch and tell a teacher about a broken step. One cares for the body and the other protects everyone using the steps.

criteria.description: Chooses a suitable personal hygiene practice and says who does it.
Chooses a safe shared-space action and assigns adult help when needed.

skills.description: Recognise the examples and vocabulary in the lesson.
Explain meanings and connections in an example.
Communicate understanding through a performance, drawing or demonstration.

spec.difficultyPlan: 5 foundational, 7 simple-use, 5 application and 3 challenge questions.
